claims.text: Adding Cr to a high-entropy alloy can be used to provide oxidation resistance.
A Si-20Cr-20Fe coating can be applied to a refractory high-entropy alloy by a fused slurry method.
The Si-20Cr-20Fe coating enhances the oxidation resistance of the refractory high-entropy alloy.
A Ni-, Co-, and Fe-rich high-entropy alloy can contain Al, Ti, and Nb as precipitation-strengthening additions.
The Ni-, Co-, and Fe-rich example is a refractory high-entropy alloy.
The initial alloy has only moderate oxidation resistance in its standard composition.
Adding Cr to the bulk or applying the Si-20Cr-20Fe coating promotes formation of a protective oxide scale.
Protective oxide formation and stability are critical in oxidative environments typically above 800 °C.
The intervention forms a continuous, dense protective surface layer such as Cr2O3, Al2O3, or silicide-derived oxides.
Oxidation-resistant elements react with oxygen at elevated temperature to form adherent oxide scales.
The oxide scales act as diffusion barriers that reduce inward oxygen flux and outward metal-species diffusion.
Reduced inward and outward diffusion slows the overall oxidation kinetics.
Modified samples will have lower oxidation mass gain and less high-temperature degradation than unmodified samples.
The untreated or baseline alloy has a higher oxidation rate because it forms a less effective oxide scale.
The benefit depends on the protective oxide scale remaining stable at high temperature.
Processing details and oxide-scale spallation can limit the efficacy of the intervention.
The magnitude of improvement can vary with alloy composition, coating uniformity, and oxidation-test conditions.
A controlled comparison at 1000 °C using mass gain, SEM/EDS, and XRD can test the hypothesis.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant reduction in mass gain or a continuous protective scale in modified samples would falsify the hypothesis.
